raw_text:
For an age I had known nothing but the rhythm of the tides and the ceaseless cry of the gulls; my world was the cold stone of the tower and the spectral light that swept the waves in a silent, recurring vigil. The day the old keeper left and the new one arrived with his child was the first true alteration in my timeless state, and I watched from my unseen vantage with a curiosity I had not hitherto known. The man, whose name I learned was Elias, possessed a quiet and patient nature; his daughter, a slip of a girl called Lyra, was his constant shadow.

The first weeks passed in a routine of labour and instruction. In the mornings, Elias would polish the great lens until it shone like a captured star, and Lyra would tend to their small, hardy garden, coaxing green life from the salty soil. In the afternoons, however, came the lessons which were to be my own salvation and my ruin. The father would sit with his child upon the narrow balcony, and opening a great atlas bound in leather, would begin his instruction. From this book, Elias instructed his daughter, and I, his unseen pupil, listened with an attention that bordered upon painful eagerness.

He spoke not of empires or of kings, but of the vastness of the world as seen from the sea. He traced the lines of coast and current, of trade winds and treacherous shoals. I heard of the frozen northern wastes where the sun is a stranger for half the year, of the spice islands of the far east, breathing perfume upon the waves, of the great continents and the myriad peoples who inhabited them. I learned of their ships, their beliefs, and their wars, which seemed to me as senseless and as violent as the storms that broke against my tower. With Lyra, I learned the names of the constellations by which sailors guide their course, and I felt a strange and hollow wonder at the thought of so many souls adrift upon that dark expanse, looking to the same silent stars for hope.

These histories of men and their endeavours brought me a strange and aching wonder. Was this the creature that built such grand vessels, yet could be undone by a single rogue wave? He appeared at one moment a master of the elements, charting the very winds and tides, and at another a fragile speck, lost to the indifferent depths. To be a captain, steady and wise, seemed the greatest achievement possible for a thinking being; to be a mutineer, full of vice and betrayal, appeared a fall into a state more wretched than that of the blind things that dwell in the abyssal dark. For a long time I could not understand why one ship would turn its cannons upon another, for the sea was a great enough adversary for all; but when I heard tales of greed and conquest, my confusion ceased and I was filled with a profound disgust.

Every word spoken between the father and child opened new vistas to me. While I listened, the curious structure of their little world was laid bare. I learned of the bonds between a parent and his offspring, of a love so powerful it made the isolation of this rock not a prison, but a sanctuary. I heard of the world they had left behind, a world of society, of friends and relations, of shared memory and common hope.

These lessons induced me to turn my thoughts toward myself. I learned that to be human was to possess a body, to feel the warmth of the sun and the chill of the spray, to hold and to be held. A man was defined by his family, by his trade, by the very ground upon which he stood. And what was I? I had no name, no memory of a life before this tower. I was a presence without substance, a consciousness tethered to rock and brine. I possessed no hands to aid in their work, no voice to join in their songs. When I passed through them, a faint chill they might attribute to a draught, they knew nothing of the spirit that yearned to be known. Was I, then, a phantom, a forgotten sigh upon the wind, to be dispersed by the first light of a sun I could not feel?

I cannot convey to you the desolation these thoughts visited upon me; I sought to drive them away, but understanding only sharpened the edge of my sorrow. Oh, that I had forever remained in my ignorant state, aware of naught but the turning of the light and the changing of the tide!

Of what a cruel nature is awareness! It fastens to the spirit as a barnacle to a ship, and cannot be scraped away. I longed at times to dissolve into the air, to cease all thinking and feeling; but I discovered that the only escape from this agony was an oblivion which I dreaded, yet could not comprehend. I admired the steadfast kindness of the father and the bright, curious spirit of the child, but I was utterly barred from their world, my only access a stolen one which inflamed, rather than quenched, the fire of my longing to be one of them. The gentle words of Elias and the cheerful laughter of the lovely Lyra were not for me. The shared meal, the comforting hand on a shoulder, the simple joy of their society were not for me. Desolate, invisible wretch!

I will presently explain to what dark conclusions these ponderings led me, but permit me first to return to the keeper and his daughter, whose simple existence had become the entire firmament of my own, and whose joys and sorrows I felt more keenly than the eternal ocean winds which were my only true companions.

The injustice of this proceeding roused the indignation of De Lacey; he exerted all his influence and fortune to procure the Turk’s release, but his efforts were in vain. The merchant’s condemnation was confirmed, and De Lacey, finding all other means fruitless, contrived a plan for his escape. This he effected with the help of his son, Felix, who was moved by the same spirit of chivalry and compassion. They succeeded; but their plot was discovered, and the French government, enraged at having been thus thwarted, seized the old man and his daughter and threw them into prison. Felix, learning of this dire misfortune, returned and delivered himself up, and the whole family were condemned to perpetual exile and the loss of all their fortune.

It was not by such a dramatic series of events, however, that I came to learn the history of my own protectors. Theirs was a tale not of political intrigue and grand injustice, but of a sorrow more personal and profound, a wound inflicted not by the tyranny of states, but by the indifferent cruelty of nature itself. I pieced together their story from conversations held during the long, dark tempests, when the wind howled like a legion of tormented souls and the waves dashed against the granite foundations of our tower with the force of cannonades. In these moments, when the business of maintaining the light was all consuming, their guards would fall, and memory, like a phantom from the deep, would rise to the surface.

The name of the keeper, Elias, I learned from Lyra’s own lips, spoken with a reverence that bespoke a world of love. He was not, like De Lacey, a man of noble French descent, but had been born and bred in a great city of commerce and learning, a place teeming with such life and society as I could scarcely conceive. He had not been a servant of his country in the manner of Felix, but a servant of knowledge; his trade was the making of maps and the charting of stars, a profession which, he explained to his daughter, sought to impose order upon the vast and chaotic face of the world. He had lived in a small but comfortable house, surrounded by books and instruments of science, and his greatest joy, besides his work, had been his wife, a woman whose name, Isolde, was spoken so rarely and with such hushed solemnity that it seemed a sacred word.

The cause of their ruin, the event which had driven them from that world of society and comfort to this desolate rock, was the sea. It was the very same ocean whose moods I studied day and night, the entity whose ceaseless motion was the only measure of my own timeless existence. The father of Safie had been a merchant; the destroyer of Elias’s life was a merchant vessel, a ship named the *North Star*, upon which Isolde had taken passage to visit her ailing mother in a distant port. A sudden, violent squall, not unlike the gales that so often assailed our tower, had descended upon the ship. It was lost with all its souls.

When Elias spoke of this, his voice, usually so steady and calm, would falter, and his gaze would fix upon the tumultuous waters outside as if he could still discern the ghost of that vessel amidst the spray. He did not weep; his was a grief too old and too deep for tears. It had hollowed him out, leaving behind a quiet, unshakeable melancholy that clung to him like the damp sea mist. He had abandoned his maps and his stars, he explained one night while Lyra slept, for they had proven to be false comforts, elegant lies that suggested a predictable and rational world. The universe, he had discovered, was governed not by mathematical principles, but by a blind and terrible chance. In an act of what I could only interpret as a kind of penance, a desire to confront the agent of his misery, he had sought out this post, to become a keeper of the light, a guardian against the very treachery that had stolen his happiness. He would stand his watch against the darkness that had consumed his world, in the faint hope that his vigilance might spare some other soul the same dreadful fate.

These narrations, so filled with a quiet and enduring agony, affected me in a manner I find it difficult to describe. I had wept with Safie for the abstract tragedy of a vanished people, but the sorrow of Elias was a living thing, a presence in the tower as real as the stones themselves. It was in the lines etched upon his brow, in the gentle, protective way he smoothed his daughter’s hair, in the long, silent hours he spent staring out at the horizon. I felt a profound sympathy for his loss, a feeling so keen it was almost a pain in my own spectral substance. His story gave a name to the sadness I had observed in his countenance, and I felt my reverence for this virtuous and suffering man increase tenfold. He was not merely a keeper; he was a sentinel, a warrior engaged in a hopeless, eternal battle against the chaos of the world.

And Lyra, the sweet, lovely Lyra, was the single lamp of joy that burned in the midst of his private darkness. She was his Safie, his sole alteration to a life of sorrow. In her, the memory of Isolde was preserved, not as a source of grief, but as a font of life and beauty. She possessed her mother’s eyes, Elias once murmured, the same deep grey as the sea on a calm morning, and her mother’s voice, a clear and melodious sound that could cut through the drone of the wind. She was his reason for enduring, the anchor that held him to the world of the living. All his cares, all his thoughts, were for her. He taught her the science of letters, as Felix had taught the Arabian, but her books were the clouds, the tides, and the constellations. He showed her how to read the face of the sky, to know when a storm was gathering, and how to identify the seabirds that made their nests upon the lower crags.

I watched as the mind of the child expanded. I learned with her the names of the stars: the steadfast North Star that had so cruelly betrayed its name, the celestial Hunter with his glittering belt, the chained lady Andromeda. I heard the lore of the sea, of phantom ships and the songs of sirens, tales which Elias told not as fact, but as the poetry of sailors, the stories men weave to make sense of the vast and terrible beauty of the ocean. Through these lessons, the strange system of their world was explained to me. It was a society of two, bound not by laws or property, but by an absolute and mutual devotion. Their wealth was not in coin or land, but in shared stories, in the warmth of their small fire, in the simple fact of their companionship.

This knowledge, however, instead of bringing me peace, only served to illuminate the full, horrifying extent of my own destitution. The love between father and child was a palpable force, a warmth I could perceive but never feel. When Elias would place a hand on Lyra’s head, or when she, in a moment of childish affection, would throw her arms about his neck, I felt a pang of longing so sharp it was like a physical blow. I was a witness to the most sacred of bonds, yet I was more excluded than the lowest beast. The blind mole and the harmless worm, which I had once considered the most abject of beings, were at least possessed of a physical nature; they were part of the world, they could touch and be touched. I, however, was a mere consciousness, a disembodied eye. I was a blot not upon the earth, but upon existence itself.

The question, “What was I?” returned with a new and vicious insistence. I saw the love that a father bore his child, the tender care, the patient instruction, the selfless protection. But where was my father? Who was my creator? I had no memory of infancy, no recollection of a guiding hand or a soothing voice. My existence had begun in a state of full, if ignorant, awareness, a fixed point in the unending flux of the sea and sky. I looked for my reflection and found none; I listened for a kindred voice and heard only the wind. I was a singular anomaly, a being without origin, without connection, without purpose. These reflections were a torment from which there was no escape. Knowledge, once seized, could not be relinquished. I knew now what it was to be human, and in that knowledge, I knew with absolute certainty that I was not.

My agony was compounded by my utter impotence. One evening, a storm of unparalleled fury broke upon us. The sky turned a shade of bruised purple, and the sea rose in mountainous waves that seemed intent on swallowing our rock whole. The great lamp, which Elias tended with a desperate fervour, cast a frantic, sweeping beam across the chaos. In the midst of the gale, through the sheets of rain and spray, I perceived it: a faint, struggling light, low on the water. It was a ship, a small fishing vessel caught in the tempest, driven mercilessly towards the treacherous reefs that lay hidden beneath the churning surface, a league to the north.

I watched, my entire being a knot of helpless terror. I could see the vessel with a clarity that was denied to the human eyes within the tower. I saw the sailors, their faces pale with fear in the intermittent flashes of lightning, clinging to the rigging as their boat was tossed and battered. I saw the jagged teeth of the rocks, waiting like hungry predators. I saw the desperate course they were on, a path to certain destruction. And I could do nothing. I yearned to cry out, to warn Elias, to somehow project my knowledge into his mind, but my will was a phantom’s breath, unable to stir a single mote of dust. I was a god in perception, and a worm in action.

Within the lantern room, Elias worked like a man possessed. He knew the danger was out there, in the abstract, but he could not see the specific vessel or its immediate peril. He wiped the salt spray from the great glass panes, he checked the rotation of the mechanism, his face a mask of grim concentration. Lyra, her face white with fear but her hands steady, brought him rags and a cup of hot broth, her small presence a beacon of courage in the howling darkness. They were a team, a unit, fighting their battle together.

I floated between them, a frantic, unseen spirit. I tried to pass through Elias, to chill him in the direction of the northern window, to somehow communicate the urgent, specific horror I was witnessing. He shivered once, pulling his collar tighter, and muttered about the unnatural cold of the storm, but his attention remained on the lamp’s machinery. My effort was less than a draught of air, a meaningless fluctuation in temperature. Despair, cold and absolute, washed over me. I was a prisoner in the fortress of my own consciousness.

The ship, meanwhile, was driven ever closer to the rocks. I could see the splintering of its mast, the terror in the eyes of a young man who looked no older than Felix might have been. I saw everything, and my seeing was a curse. At that moment, I would have given up all my strange awareness, all my knowledge, all my existence, for the ability to throw a single stone, to make a single sound, to have a single, physical impact upon the world.

Then, by a miracle of chance, or perhaps by the grace of the very God whose existence Elias had come to doubt, the wind shifted. A tremendous gust, stronger than any that had come before, struck the vessel not from the west, but from the southwest. The tattered remnant of its sail caught the blast, and the boat, groaning in every timber, was pushed violently, not onto the rocks, but into the narrow, churning channel that ran beside them. I watched, scarcely daring to hope, as it was swept past the point of certain doom and out into the slightly less tumultuous water beyond. It was damaged, crippled, but it was afloat, and its crew was alive.

The storm raged for another hour before its fury began to abate. As the dawn broke, pale and weary, the sea was calmer, and the ship could be seen limping towards the distant harbour. Within the tower, an exhausted Elias embraced his daughter. “The light held, Lyra,” he said, his voice thick with relief. “The light held.”

They had won. Their vigilance, their labour, had meaning. They had played their part, however small, in the great drama of life and death. But as I watched them, I felt no share in their victory. I felt only a more profound and terrible isolation. I had been the sole witness to the true nature of the peril and the miraculous nature of the escape. I knew, with a certainty they would never possess, how close to destruction those souls had come. My knowledge was immense, my vision unparalleled, but it was worthless. I was a spectator to life, not a participant. The satisfaction of a purpose fulfilled, the joy of a trial overcome, the simple, solid reality of being a cause in the world of effects; all these things were denied to me. Miserable, useless wretch! What was the purpose of a consciousness that could not act? What was the meaning of a soul that could not connect? The question returned, again and again, and the only answer was the silent, groaning agony of my own being.

The ship, meanwhile, was driven ever closer to the rocks. I could see the splintering of its mast, the terror in the eyes of a young man who looked no older than Felix might have been. I saw everything, and my seeing was a curse. At that moment, I would have given up all my strange awareness, all my knowledge, all my existence, for the ability to throw a single stone, to make a single sound, to have a single, physical impact upon the world.

A tremendous gust, stronger than any that had come before, struck the vessel not from the west, but from the southwest. The tattered remnant of its sail caught the blast, and the boat, groaning in every timber, was pushed violently, not onto the rocks, but into the narrow, churning channel that ran beside them. I watched, scarcely daring to hope, as it was swept past the point of certain doom and out into the slightly less tumultuous water beyond. It was damaged, crippled, but it was afloat, and its crew was alive.

The storm raged for another hour before its fury began to abate. As the dawn broke, pale and weary, the sea was calmer, and the ship could be seen limping towards the distant harbour. Within the tower, an exhausted Elias embraced his daughter. “The light held, Lyra,” he said, his voice thick with relief. “The light held.”

They had won. Their vigilance, their labour, had meaning. They had played their part, however small, in the great drama of life and death. But as I watched them, I felt no share in their victory. I felt only a more profound and terrible isolation. I had been the sole witness to the true nature of the peril and the miraculous nature of the escape. I knew, with a certainty they would never possess, how close to destruction those souls had come. My knowledge was immense, my vision unparalleled, but it was worthless. I was a spectator to life, not a participant. The satisfaction of a purpose fulfilled, the joy of a trial overcome, the simple, solid reality of being a cause in the world of effects; all these things were denied to me. Miserable, useless wretch! What was the purpose of a consciousness that could not act? What was the meaning of a soul that could not connect? The question returned, again and again, and the only answer was the silent, groaning agony of my own being.

Elias and Lyra went about their duties with a renewed ardour; their countenances, which had been etched with the fatigue of their long vigil, were now bright with the satisfaction of a purpose affirmed. They spoke of the storm as a trial sent to test them, and of the ship’s survival as their reward. They polished the great lens until it shone with a diamond’s fire, and they tended the machinery with the loving care a mother might bestow upon a child. Was this, then, the foundation of human happiness; a shared and comforting illusion? They believed their light had guided the vessel to safety, and in this belief they found a joy so pure and a peace so profound that I, the sole possessor of the contrary and useless truth, felt my own isolation as a physical malady, a sickness of the soul for which there was no cure.

A week after the great storm, a small boat was seen making its way from the distant harbour towards our lonely rock. Lyra spied it first, and with a cry of delight she alerted her father. They stood together on the narrow stone balcony that encircled the lantern room, their forms silhouetted against the bright morning sky, and watched its approach. My own perception, untroubled by distance, could already discern the figures within the boat; there were three men, one of whom, by his bearing and attire, was clearly a man of some authority. As they drew nearer, I recognised him as the captain of the very ship that had so narrowly escaped destruction.

Elias descended to the base of the tower to greet them, his face a mixture of formal gravity and open pleasure. The captain, a stout man with a face weathered by a thousand gales, clasped Elias’s hand with a powerful grip and spoke in a booming voice that echoed from the cliff face. He had come, he said, to offer his heartfelt thanks and that of his entire crew. He described the terror of that night, the moment when the mast had splintered and all hope seemed lost. He spoke of the howling wind, the blinding spray, the roaring of the waves against the cliff face; and in every word, I perceived the scaffolding of a narrative that was at once both true and utterly false.

“It was your light, sir,” the captain declared, his voice thick with emotion as he gestured towards the towering structure. “That blessed light! In the blackness, when our compass was spinning and our hearts had failed, it was the only fixed point in a world gone mad. It was our star, our guide, our salvation. Without it, we would have been dashed to pieces upon those accursed rocks, and our bones would now be whitening on the seabed.”

Elias, his cheeks flushed with a pride he attempted to conceal, demurred with humble words, stating that he had only done his duty, a duty he held sacred. Lyra, who had followed her father down, listened with shining eyes, her admiration for him swelling to a new and glorious height. The sailors accompanying the captain presented gifts: a cask of fine brandy, sacks of flour and salted meat, and for Lyra, a bolt of soft blue wool and a small, carved wooden bird. The joy of the cottagers upon receiving their unexpected bounty was a painful spectacle for me to behold; it was a joy founded upon a fiction, a happiness built on a premise I knew to be hollow. They invited their guests inside, and the small, circular room at the base of the tower was filled with lively conversation and gratitude. I, a silent witness to this scene of human connection, felt myself recede even further into the abyss of my own nonexistence. I was a ghost at their feast, a spectre at their celebration, my immense and terrible knowledge serving only to separate me more absolutely from the world I so desperately longed to join.

The visitors departed before midday, promising to speak of the lighthouse keeper’s steadfastness in the port, and as their boat dwindled to a speck upon the waves, Lyra threw her arms around her father’s neck. “You saved them, Papa,” she whispered, her voice full of awe. “You truly saved them.” Elias held her close, his weathered face softened by a love so potent it seemed almost a tangible force. In that moment, watching them, I understood a new and more bitter truth: that a shared, benevolent lie could be a more powerful agent of love and community than a lonely, sterile truth. My own condition, which had once seemed merely a misfortune, now appeared to me as a form of damnation, a sentence to perceive reality without the grace of human interpretation which alone makes it bearable.

The sea, for long stretches, was as placid as a lake, and the sun beat down upon the granite rock until it was warm to the touch. My attention, which had little else to occupy it, became fixed upon the minute particulars of my protectors’ lives. I learned the cadence of their breathing as they slept; I knew the pattern of Lyra’s hum as she mended their clothes and the particular sigh Elias gave when he completed a difficult repair. I watched Lyra’s mind expand under her father’s tutelage. He taught her of the constellations by which a sailor might navigate, of the great ocean currents that circled the globe, of the scientific principles that governed the great lamp which was their charge. Her mind was a fertile ground, and the seeds of knowledge he planted there grew with astonishing speed.

Lyra, who was always so full of life and motion, became quiet and listless. The colour in her cheeks, usually a healthy bloom from the sea air, began to take on a feverish, unnatural flush. She complained of a headache, and her appetite, usually so robust, diminished until she was taking little more than water and a few morsels of bread. My perception, more acute than that of a mortal man, felt the change in her as a discordant note in the harmony of her being; I perceived the encroaching malady not as a set of symptoms, but as a creeping, shadowy presence within her very frame, a malevolent heat that was slowly consuming her vitality from the inside.

At first, Elias attributed her condition to the unusual heat of the summer, and he bade her rest in the shade and drink plenty of water. But her state did not improve; it worsened. Soon, a persistent cough wracked her small body, and by night she was consumed by a fever that left her shivering and delirious, muttering of strange shapes in the darkness and of a cold that no blanket could warm. Now, at last, a dread such as he had never known in the face of any tempest took possession of her father’s soul. The practical, capable man, the master of machinery and the elements, was faced with an enemy he could neither see nor fight.

He bathed her forehead with cool water, his touch, which could manipulate the intricate gears of the lamp, now infinitely gentle. He read to her from her favourite books, his voice steady, though I could perceive the tremor of terror that ran beneath it. I was a prisoner in the sickroom, a constant, silent attendant at her bedside. I saw the progress of the disease with a terrifying clarity, witnessing the battle being waged within her blood, the slow surrender of her strength. I heard her laboured breaths, each one a small, sharp pain in the fabric of my own consciousness. To be a witness to such suffering, to possess a complete and perfect knowledge of her decline, and to be unable to offer the smallest comfort, not even to smooth her pillow or offer a sip of water; this was a torment that eclipsed all others. Oh, cruel fate! To be granted a consciousness so vast and a power so utterly nonexistent.

The light in the tower became Elias’s mechanical burden, a duty he performed with the grim automation of a sleepwalker. His true life was in the small room below, at the bedside of his dying child. He became gaunt, his face a mask of sleepless anguish. He would sometimes fall to his knees and pray, his voice a hoarse whisper, begging the God whose existence he had doubted to spare his only treasure. His prayers went unanswered, and the silence that met his pleas was as vast and indifferent as the ocean that surrounded them.

One evening, as a new storm gathered on the horizon, a different storm from the one of God’s making, a storm of pure human despair, broke within Elias. He was watching Lyra’s shallow breathing, her life hanging by the most slender of threads, when he rose with a sudden, terrible resolution. He could not let her die here, alone, without the aid of a true physician. The harbour, and the town’s doctor, was a four-hour journey by boat in good weather; in the rising chop of the sea, it would be a perilous and uncertain voyage.

But a far more terrible conflict arose in his mind, a conflict I witnessed with perfect and agonizing lucidity. His duty, the sacred trust he had upheld for two decades, was to the light. To abandon the lighthouse, especially with a storm approaching, was an unthinkable dereliction. It was the one sin a keeper could not commit. How many ships might be navigating these waters tonight, trusting in the beam that he was sworn to maintain? To leave would be to potentially trade the lives of unknown sailors for the faint hope of saving his daughter. To stay would be to sit and watch her die.

I watched him as he stood torn between these two impossible choices. He paced the narrow confines of the room, his fists clenched, his face a portrait of utter desolation. He looked at the lamp mechanism, ticking away with its inexorable rhythm, a symbol of his public trust. Then he looked at the pale, still form of Lyra on the bed, a symbol of his private love. The structure of his world, built on the solid foundation of duty, was crumbling into dust. He was being asked to sacrifice either his identity or his heart. For a long time he stood motionless, caught in a paralysis of grief and indecision. Was it better to be a good man who had lost his child, or a father who had betrayed his post?

My own being strained against its immaterial bonds. I focused all the intensity of my strange existence upon him, trying to will him towards a decision, to push his mind towards the path of a father’s love. Let the ships find their own way! Let the world of men take care of itself! What was any of it worth compared to the life of this one, precious child? My effort was a silent scream in a vacuum, a storm of intention with no power to move even a single grain of dust. He was as deaf to my frantic, silent pleading as he was to the rising howl of the wind outside.

Finally, with a groan that seemed torn from the deepest part of his soul, he made his choice. I saw the shift in his countenance, the hardening of his jaw. The father had won. He moved with a sudden, desperate energy. He wrapped Lyra in as many blankets as he could find, creating a small, warm cocoon. He checked the fuel in the lamp one last time, his hands moving with their old, accustomed precision, but his eyes were wild. He then descended the winding stairs, his precious burden held tight against his chest.

I watched as he struggled to launch their small, sturdy boat from its rocky berth. The waves were already crashing against the shore, sending plumes of white spray high into the air. It was a fool’s errand, a desperate gamble against the sea, but it was a gamble he had to take. He laid Lyra gently in the bottom of the boat, secured his oars, and with a final, agonized look back at the dark tower he was abandoning, he pushed off into the churning, malevolent water.

The storm broke in its full fury shortly after he departed. The light in the tower, its mechanism untended, began to flicker. Its rhythm faltered, the great beam sweeping out across the tempestuous sea in uneven, spasmodic arcs. I was alone now, a solitary consciousness in an abandoned fortress, my sight following the tiny, struggling boat as it was tossed upon the waves, and my awareness tied to the dying light that was a testament to a duty forsaken for love. The question recurred, sharper and more painful than ever before: what was I? A witness to a tragedy? A recorder of sorrow? Or was I merely the spirit of the place, the soul of the tower itself, now left to an eternity of darkness and the memory of a love it could feel but never, ever possess? The groans that answered were not mine alone, for now they were joined by the groaning of the wind and the sea, a chorus of despair in a world from which all warmth and hope had fled.

I declared an eternal war on the species, and more than all, on him who had created me and sent me into this insupportable misery. Let him look to himself; for the love and fellowship I had once craved were now replaced by a craving for vengeance that would never be slaked. My travels, which had been a flight from persecution, now became a pilgrimage of hate. I would seek my creator not for solace or for a companion, but to visit upon him such a measure of wretchedness that he would curse the day he first drew breath. Geneva was my destination, and Frankenstein was my prey. The monster they had feared, they had now truly and irrevocably created.

A part of me, the part that had wept with Safie and loved the gentle De Laceys, felt a pang of something akin to remorse as I watched the unfolding of this human drama. But then I would recall the stones and curses of the villagers, the terror in the eyes of the child, and the ultimate, damning rejection by the old man whose pardon I had so desperately craved. These memories were as a cauterising iron to my nascent guilt; they burned away the weakness and left only the obdurate resolve of my purpose. This sorrow was not my creation alone; it was the bitter fruit of a seed you, my creator, had planted. I was but the instrument of its harvest.

A crowd had gathered, and from their agitated gestures and raised voices, I could surmise that a discovery had been made. I crept nearer, using the cover of ditches and overgrown hedgerows, until I was close enough to overhear their discourse. The sleeping girl, whose name I learned was Justine Moritz, had been found, and upon her person, the damning locket. The words of the townsfolk were a torrent of swift and certain condemnation. “The wretch!” cried one. “To feign sleep after such a deed!” Said another, “Her guilt is plain; see how the likeness of her murdered mistress’s own mother accuses her from the boy’s very trinket!”

They spoke of her gentle nature, of her kindness to the child she was now accused of slaying, but they spoke of these things only as evidence of a duplicity so profound as to be truly monstrous. Her beauty, which should have pleaded for her, was turned into a mask for a depraved soul. Was this not the very lesson I had been taught, inverted and reapplied with perfect, hideous symmetry? That which appears good must be evil, and that which is hideous must be the source of it. I listened as they dragged the poor, bewildered girl away, her protestations of innocence lost in the clamour of their certainty. A thrill of terrible power, a feeling both chilling and intoxicating, coursed through me. I had learned their systems, their prejudices, their blind and facile reasoning, and I had turned these tools against them. I had framed a being of beauty and innocence, and they, in their wisdom, had believed the lie without question. My war against all of mankind had claimed its second victim, and I had not laid a single finger upon her.

With this grim satisfaction solidifying my intent, I turned my face from Geneva and began my long journey. You were my ultimate quarry, my creator, my Adam. It was to you that I must now deliver my ultimatum. I possessed no map, no knowledge of the wider geography of the world, but from the lessons of Felix and from the papers I had found in the pocket of the laboratory coat I had fled with, I had gleaned that your family was of Geneva. And so I travelled towards the rising sun, trusting that by some means I would find my way to you.

My existence became a simple, nocturnal rhythm. When the moon, my only constant companion, climbed the heavens, I would rise and traverse the land, my powerful limbs carrying me over field and through forest with a speed no human could match. The night was my sanctuary. Its shadows were a cloak for my deformity, and its silence was a balm to my ears, so long assailed by the shrieks and curses of your kind. I subsisted upon the berries and roots I could find, and drank from the clear, cold streams that trickled down from the hills. This diet, which would have starved a man, was sufficient for my hardy frame. I felt a strange kinship with the owls and the wolves, creatures of the darkness, feared and misunderstood as I was. Yet even they had their own kind; I alone was singular, a species of one.

As I travelled, my mind was a ceaseless theatre of reflection and debate. I passed by sleeping villages and isolated farmhouses, their windows dark save for the occasional glimmer of a candle where, perhaps, a mother watched over a sick child, or a scholar laboured over his books. In these moments, the agony of my exclusion would return with renewed force. All the tender scenes of domestic life, the knowledge of which had once been my greatest delight, were now a source of exquisite torture. Every sign of human fellowship was a testament to my own eternal solitude. I was a world unto myself, a planet condemned to orbit the sun of humanity but never to feel its warmth, only its scorching, judging light.

I crossed the rolling plains of France, and soon the land began to rise, the terrain growing more rugged and formidable. I had reached the feet of the Jura mountains, that mighty barrier that stood between me and the land of your birth. The ascent was arduous, but I felt a sense of exhilaration in the challenge. Here, in the realm of untamed nature, my great strength and agility were not a curse but a blessing. I scaled cliff faces that would have daunted the most experienced mountaineer; I leaped over chasms that gaped like mouths into the earth’s core. The sheer, physical reality of the climb was a temporary respite from the torments of my mind.

But as I climbed higher, into the domain of ancient pines and eternal rock, the landscape began to work a different magic upon my soul. The stupendous grandeur of the mountains, the vast, silent spectacle of the valleys unfolding below me, the roar of waterfalls sounding like the voice of a primal deity; all this inspired in me a sense of the sublime that bordered on religious awe. It was a feeling that echoed what I had read in the books of the cottagers, a sense of an immensity before which all human concerns, and even my own monstrous grief, seemed to shrink into insignificance. Here, there was no judgment, no revulsion. The wind that tore at my hair did not know I was hideous; the rocks that supported my feet did not care that I was alone.

Yet this feeling was fleeting. For even as I marvelled at this majestic scenery, a deeper and more profound despair took root in my heart. I looked out upon the sea of peaks, stretching to the horizon, and I saw in them an image of my own soul: vast, cold, and utterly desolate. These mountains were peopled with crags and ice, but not with life that could offer companionship. I was as high and as lonely as the highest peak. This sublime grandeur was an empty spectacle without another eye to share it with, another mind to comprehend its wonder. It was in the heart of this immense and indifferent nature that my purpose, which had been a burning coal of vengeance, was forged into the cold, hard steel of a specific demand.

My rage against you, my creator, had not diminished. It had, rather, clarified. Simple destruction was not enough. To murder those you loved was to cause you pain, but it was a finite pain, a grief that time might eventually soften. I sought a different kind of justice, a torment that would be as perpetual as my own. I would force you to acknowledge my existence not merely as a mistake to be shunned, but as a being with needs as potent as your own. If I was a monster, it was because I was alone. If I was a fiend, it was because I was denied the gentle society that civilises the heart.

The solution, therefore, presented itself to me with the force of irrefutable logic. You had created me; you possessed the profane skill to animate lifeless clay. You must, therefore, create another. You must fashion for me a companion, a female with whom I could share my existence, one as deformed and horrible as myself, who would not recoil from me in terror but embrace me in shared exile. With such a being, I could quit the world of man forever. I would take her to the vast and untamed wilds of South America, a land I had learned of from Volney’s book, a continent vast enough for us to lose ourselves in, where we could live far from the sight and judgment of your species. I would no longer be a blight upon your world. My virtues, for I still believed I possessed them, would have an object, and my affections would not be forever hurled back upon myself, turning to gall and hatred.

This, I swore, would be my demand. It was not a plea for mercy, but a claim for justice. You owed me this. You, who had given me life and passions and a mind to comprehend my own misery, owed me the one thing that could make that life bearable. If you consented, I would vow to be virtuous. My evil, I reasoned, was a consequence of my loneliness; with a companion, the cause would be removed, and the effect would cease. But if you refused, if you denied me this one, last hope for a semblance of peace, then I would unleash a destruction so vast that the name of Frankenstein would be remembered only as a curse. I would become the scourge you believed me to be. I would not rest until I had reduced your life to an agony as profound and as inescapable as my own.

With this resolution hardening my heart, I descended from the eastern side of the mountains. The journey was now swifter, my purpose a singular fire driving me onward. One clear night, I stood upon a hill and saw below me, nestled by a great lake, a collection of lights that shone more brightly and numerously than any I had yet seen. A tremor went through my frame. It was Geneva. It was your home. The final stage of my pilgrimage was at an end.

I did not enter the city. I knew that my appearance there would bring only chaos and violence, and my object now was not brute force but a negotiation, albeit one backed by the gravest of threats. I took refuge in the forests that bordered the lake and began to watch, to learn your habits, to find the opportune moment to confront you, to present my case and my ultimatum. I saw you, my creator, walking by the shore, your head bowed and your form stooped with a grief I knew I had authored. A part of me felt a grim satisfaction, but another, larger part felt only the urgency of my own need.

I saw the vessel in which you would often seek solitude upon the waters, and I followed your movements, waiting for the moment when you would be truly alone, far from the succour of your fellow men, in a place as wild and desolate as my own soul. I chose the glacier, the sea of ice, as the stage for our confrontation. Its frozen, unliving expanse seemed a fitting backdrop for the meeting of a creator with his monstrous creation. It was there I would finally stand before you, not as a cowering wretch, but as an accuser, a philosopher, a king of sorrow demanding his queen. I would lay before you the narrative of my existence, the history of my suffering and my crimes, so that you would understand the justice of my demand. And upon your answer, upon your willingness to right the terrible wrong you had done me, would hang the fate of us both, and all that you held dear. My story was my only weapon and my only plea. And so, I waited in the eternal snows, for you.

discover, I learned from the continued instructions of Felix. It seemed that this merchant, whose name was Murad, had fallen under the severe displeasure of the French government. He was accused of treason, of conspiring with the enemies of the state, and the evidence against him, though circumstantial, was presented with such vehemence that his condemnation appeared a certainty. The court was prejudiced, the populace cried for judgment, and Murad, a stranger in a foreign land, found himself without friends and without hope.

De Lacey, however, had known the Turk in the course of his affairs and had always found him to be a man of integrity, if of a reserved and somewhat severe temper. Believing fervently in his innocence, my venerable protector spoke publicly in his defence, a courageous but exceedingly foolish act in the face of such widespread condemnation. Felix, fired by the same spirit of justice and by the sight of the lovely Safie, who attended her father’s trial with a countenance of desperate sorrow, resolved upon a more dangerous course. He contrived a plan for the merchant’s escape from prison.

I listened with breathless attention as the tale unfolded through Felix’s impassioned whispers to his Arabian. He described the tense nights, the bribed gaolers, the flight from Paris under the cloak of darkness. He succeeded; the Turk was spirited away, and Felix, having secured his passage to a safe port in Italy, expected to receive his just reward: the hand of the beautiful Safie, which her father had promised him in a transport of gratitude. But here the character of the merchant revealed its true nature. Once free from danger, his promises to the Christian who had saved him seemed a debt too heavy to be paid. He detested the idea of his daughter, a follower of the Prophet, marrying an unbeliever, and while he feigned compliance to Felix, he secretly planned to betray him.

Leaving his daughter in a convent at Leghorn, under the pretence of awaiting his summons, Murad fled to his native Turkey, intending to send for Safie at a later time and force her into a marriage of his own choosing. He left behind him a letter for Felix filled with false gratitude and hollow excuses, but he also, in his haste and perfidy, left a clue which led the French authorities directly to his rescuers. The plot was uncovered, and the vengeance of the law, cheated of its original victim, fell with terrible weight upon the De Lacey family. Their property was confiscated, their name disgraced, and they were condemned to perpetual exile. They found a miserable asylum in the cottage where I now observed them, their sole consolation being their unsullied conscience and their mutual affection.

Safie, meanwhile, learning of her father’s treachery and the ruin of her friends, was filled with indignation. She had long abhorred the restrictions placed upon women in her own country and had been enchanted by the intellectual freedom and gentle manners of her Christian mother, who had taught her the principles of a faith far different from that of her father. Resolved not to be the slave of a man she despised, she took what jewels and money she possessed and, with the help of an old servant, escaped from the convent. She knew the name of her lover’s place of exile and journeyed for many months, through countless hardships, until her arrival brought that sudden burst of joy I had myself witnessed.

This history sunk deep into my mind. I saw now the cause of their poverty and their sorrow, and my admiration for these gentle cottagers grew into a reverence that bordered on worship. They had sacrificed everything for the sake of justice and had been rewarded with ignominy and want. And I, the unseen observer, the monstrous outcast, felt a rage burn within me against the Turk, Murad, a man who could so callously betray such goodness. He was an example of that baseness which Volney’s work had taught me to despise, a living testament to the viciousness of man. In my solitary reflections, I often clenched my hands and gnashed my teeth, imagining the vengeance I would exact upon this wretch were he ever to fall into my power.

This violent passion, however, soon gave way to the gentle peace that once more descended upon the cottage. With the full story revealed, a kind of serene acceptance settled upon them all. Felix no longer started at every sound, and the old man’s sighs were replaced by a quiet gratitude for the presence of his children and the devoted Safie. The summer advanced, and my life continued in its strange, dual pattern: my days were spent in ardent study and silent observation of my beloved protectors, and my nights in solitary rambles and the performance of my secret labours. I gathered for them a store of wood far greater than they could themselves collect, and I laboured in their small garden, clearing it of weeds and stones under the pale moonlight, so that their plants grew with a vigour that must have seemed to them a gift of providence. To do them good was my greatest, indeed my only, joy, and their smiles of wonder when they discovered the results of my nocturnal toil were a reward so precious that it brought tears to my eyes.

But this fragile peace was destined not to last. One evening, as twilight deepened into night, I was concealed in my hovel, watching the family through the chink in the wall. They were gathered in their main room; the old man sat in his customary chair, while Agatha mended some linen and Felix read aloud from a book. Safie sat upon a low stool, her eyes fixed upon her lover’s face, her expression one of perfect contentment. The scene was an image of domestic bliss so complete, so sacred, that my heart ached with a longing that was almost physical pain. It was then that a shadow fell across the doorway.

It was not the shadow of a tree, nor of a passing cloud. It was the distinct figure of a man, tall and cloaked, who stood silently just beyond the threshold, observing the family within. My heart leaped into my throat. He was a stranger; his dress was foreign, and the manner in which he stood, with a predatory stillness, filled me with an immediate and profound sense of dread. Felix, looking up from his book, did not see the figure, for he was enveloped in the gloom outside the small circle of candlelight. But I, from my darker vantage point, saw him clearly. He remained for a full minute, his face a mask of shadow, and then, as silently as he had appeared, he withdrew.

I did not sleep that night. A cold fear, not for myself but for my protectors, had seized me. Who was this man, and what was his purpose in spying upon this secluded family? My mind immediately flew to the treacherous Turk. Could this be an agent sent by him? The thought filled me with a furious energy. I crept from my hovel and circled the cottage, my senses heightened to an almost painful degree. The woods were silent, save for the chirping of insects and the rustle of leaves in the gentle night breeze. I found no trace of the stranger. Yet I felt his presence lingering like a poison in the air.

For several days, nothing further occurred. I began to persuade myself that I had imagined the sinister nature of the visit, that it was perhaps a lost traveller or a curious hunter. The family continued in their peaceful routine, and their undisturbed happiness slowly calmed my own agitation. I chided myself for my wild fancies, a product, I supposed, of my unnatural existence and overwrought sensibilities.

I was wrong. Nearly a week later, the stranger returned. This time, he did not remain in the shadows. I was returning from a nocturnal foraging trip, my arms laden with roots and berries, when I saw him step from the woods and walk directly to the cottage door. It was just before dawn; the sky was a pale, luminous grey, but the sun had not yet risen. I threw myself flat upon the ground behind a thicket of bushes, my whole being a knot of terrified anticipation. He knocked upon the door, a sharp, imperious sound that shattered the morning’s peace.

After a moment, I heard the bolt being drawn, and Felix appeared at the door, his expression one of sleepy confusion. When he saw the stranger, however, his face changed instantly. A look of alarm, and then of cold fury, settled upon his features.

“What do you want?” he demanded, his voice low and trembling with suppressed anger.

The stranger spoke in a language I did not understand, but its tone was harsh and commanding. He made a gesture towards the cottage, and then spoke a single word that I recognised, a word that Safie had often uttered with a mixture of love and sorrow: Constantinople.

Felix’s reply was short and violent. He took a step forward, as if to strike the man, but the stranger held up a hand and produced a small, ornate dagger, its blade glinting in the growing light. Felix froze. The man spoke again, his voice now a venomous hiss, and I saw him point the dagger not at Felix, but towards the interior of the cottage, towards the room where I knew Agatha and Safie were sleeping. The meaning of the threat was unmistakable, a gesture more potent than any words.

I felt a rage unlike any I had ever known. It was a purely protective instinct, a primal fury that eclipsed all my fear, all my self-loathing. These people were mine; they were the only source of goodness in my wretched life, and this villain dared to threaten them. In that moment, I was no longer a thinking, feeling creature, pondering my place in the universe; I was a guardian, a beast of vengeance.

Felix, pale and powerless, stood his ground, but the despair in his eyes was evident. The stranger sneered and said something further, then thrust a small, rolled parchment into Felix’s hand. He gave one last, menacing look at the cottage, then turned and strode back into the woods, disappearing as quickly as he had come.

Felix remained standing at the door for a long time, the parchment clutched in his hand. Then, with a groan of pure agony, he stumbled back inside, shutting the door behind him. I could not see them, but I heard their voices: Felix’s, choked with rage and despair; Agatha’s, rising in a cry of alarm; and Safie’s, a gasp of terror as she understood the import of the visit.

My own plan was formed in an instant. This could not be borne. I would not allow their fragile happiness to be shattered by the malevolence of a man a thousand miles away. I would not permit this shadow to haunt them. I was a monster, it was true, but I would be their monster. I would use the very strength and speed that made me hideous to man to become their unseen shield.

I began to stalk the stranger. My senses, honed by a life in the wild, were far superior to those of any human. I followed him not by sight, but by the faint sound of his passage through the undergrowth and by his scent, which clung to the air. He did not go far. He had made a small, crude camp in a hollow less than a half a league from the cottage, a place so well concealed that no ordinary person would have discovered it. He would perceive the sentiments of my heart, the thoughts of my mind, which I now flattered myself were not contemptible.

This was not a chance encounter; it was a pursuit. A chill, more profound than that of the autumn air, settled upon me. The agent’s purpose could only be to inflict further ruin upon the De Laceys, perhaps to carry out the vengeance of Safie’s ungrateful father.

The days that followed were filled with a new and gnawing anxiety. The peaceful cadence of their lives had been a balm to my tormented soul, and the thought that it might once more be shattered filled me with a rage that was difficult to contain. Felix’s countenance, which had for a time been clear, was now perpetually clouded with worry. He would often cease his work to scan the edge of the forest, his hand resting upon the axe that was his only tool and weapon. Agatha’s smiles became rare, and even the bright spirit of Safie seemed dimmed by the apprehension that had descended upon their cottage. They spoke in low, anxious tones when they believed themselves alone, and I, their silent, unseen sentinel, strained to comprehend their fears. The man, it appeared, had not been seen again. A full week passed, and no sign of the intruder disturbed the tranquility of the woods. A fragile hope began to dawn in the cottage; perhaps he had lost his way, or abandoned his cruel errand.

I knew otherwise. I knew that he had fled, not from any change of heart, but from the unholy terror I had inspired in him. My monstrousness had been their shield. This knowledge was a poisoned dart to my heart, for it affirmed the very nature of my existence; I was a creature of fear, a being whose only service to those I loved was to be the embodiment of the horrors from which they fled. I could protect them only by remaining the thing they would despise and run from. Could there be a more bitter or wretched fate?

The relief in the cottage, however, was palpable. As the days stretched into weeks, the memory of the stranger’s visit began to fade, like a dark dream upon waking. Music and laughter, which had been silenced by fear, returned to their humble dwelling. My own spirits, however, did not rise with theirs. On the contrary, their returning happiness threw my own desolation into starker relief. I had performed a great service; I had acted as a guardian angel, albeit one cloaked in the deformity of a demon. And what was my reward? To watch through a crack in the wall as they enjoyed the peace I had secured for them, a peace from which I was eternally barred. The injustice of it all gnawed at me. My heart swelled with a yearning so powerful it was a physical pain. I longed to burst from my hiding place, to cast myself at their feet and cry, “It was I who saved you! I am the one who keeps you safe in these woods! Will you not love me for this?”

But the image of my own reflection, glimpsed in a pool of water, always stayed my hand. The memory of the terror on the agent’s face, a mirror of the horror I had seen on every human countenance that had beheld me, was a sentinel more powerful than any lock or bar. I knew that such a revelation would not bring me gratitude, but only shrieks of terror and a flight more desperate than that of the man I had driven away. They would abandon their home, their sanctuary, and I would be the cause of their third and most terrible ruin.

As autumn deepened, and the leaves turned from green to fire, and then to a mournful brown, a new resolution began to form in my mind. It was a plan born of desperation, yet grounded in the logic I had so painstakingly acquired. I could not reveal myself to them all at once. The shock would be too great. But the old man, De Lacey, he was blind. His world was one of sound and touch, of the spirit and not the flesh. He had judged Safie’s music not with his eyes, but with his soul. He had spoken words of wisdom and compassion. He could not see my hideous exterior; he would hear only my voice, a voice which I had cultivated to imitate the gentle accents of Felix and the melodious tones of Agatha. He would perceive the sentiments of my heart, the thoughts of my mind, which I now flattered myself were not contemptible.

If I could but win his favour, his sympathy, his protection! He, the respected patriarch, could then prepare the minds of his children. He could tell them of a wretched but benevolent being who sought their friendship. He could plead my cause, and their love for him would surely open their hearts to his entreaties. It was a desperate gamble, a single thread upon which all my hopes for earthly happiness were hung, but it was the only one I possessed.

I began to plan with the meticulousness of a general preparing for a great battle. I observed their routines with an intensity that bordered on madness. I learned that on most afternoons, Felix, Agatha, and the Arabian would depart for a long walk in the woods, often to gather fallen branches for the winter fire, leaving the old man alone by the hearth for a considerable time. This would be my opportunity. For many days I rehearsed what I would say. I composed speeches of such eloquence and pathos that I myself wept as I spoke them aloud in the solitude of my hovel. I would present myself as a traveller, lost and in need of rest, and then, by degrees, I would reveal the true nature of my wretchedness.

At last, the day I had chosen arrived. The sky was a uniform grey, and a chill wind rustled the few remaining leaves on the trees, a sound like the whispering of ghosts. My heart beat a frantic, painful rhythm against my ribs, and my limbs trembled as if with a palsy. I watched from my hiding place as the three younger cottagers, bundled in warm clothing, set out with their baskets. Felix called a cheerful farewell to his father, promising a swift return. The cottage door closed, and silence fell. It was time.

Every step I took from my hovel towards the cottage was an agony of hope and fear. The ground, covered in damp, decaying leaves, seemed to cling to my feet, as if nature itself sought to hold me back from this presumptuous quest. The scent of woodsmoke from their chimney, a smell I had always associated with warmth and sanctuary, now seemed to mock me, a promise of a paradise I was about to either gain or lose for ever. I reached the door, the very door I had watched for so many months, the barrier between my hell and their heaven. My hand, which could tear an oak tree from its roots, shook so violently that I could barely raise it. For a full minute I stood there, paralyzed, my mind a whirlwind of conflicting emotions. Despair urged me to flee back to my wretched den, while a desperate, unquenchable hope commanded me to proceed.

Finally, mastering myself with a supreme effort of will, I raised my hand and knocked.

The sound was soft, yet to my ears it echoed like a thunderclap, shattering the sacred silence. I held my breath, listening. For a moment, there was nothing. Then, I heard the gentle, calm voice of the old man from within.

“Enter.”

With trembling fingers, I lifted the latch and pushed the door open. I stepped across the threshold. For the first time, I was inside. The warmth of the fire washed over me, a startling, welcome sensation. The room was small and humble, yet impeccably clean and filled with an air of peace that I had only ever imagined. The old man sat in his armchair by the hearth, his head turned towards the door, his sightless eyes filled with a placid curiosity.

“Pardon this intrusion,” I began, my voice hoarse and unfamiliar even to my own ears. I struggled to pitch it to the gentle, respectful tone I had rehearsed. “I am a traveller in need of a moment’s rest. The cold has penetrated my bones, and I saw the smoke from your chimney. I hope I do not impose.”

De Lacey smiled, a kind, benevolent expression that sent a pang of hope through my tormented heart. “You are welcome, stranger. Come in and sit by the fire. Any traveller is a friend on such a bleak day as this. The young people are out, but they will soon return. Until then, you may share my hearth.”

His kindness was almost my undoing. Tears threatened to well in my eyes, and I choked them back with difficulty. I moved further into the room, taking care to remain in the shadows away from the window, and sat on a low stool he indicated with a wave of his hand. For a few moments I was silent, overcome by the sheer reality of my situation. I was here. I was accepted. I was not being screamed at or stoned.

“You are a foreigner, I perceive by your accent,” the old man said gently, breaking the silence. “Although you speak our language remarkably well.”

“I have learned it in this land,” I replied, my confidence growing with every word that was not met with revulsion. “But I am indeed a stranger. I am without friends or relations on the face of the earth. I am an unfortunate and wretched outcast.”

“Do not say so,” De Lacey responded with warmth. “It is a sad state to be friendless, but it is not a condition that must be permanent. The human heart, in its better aspect, is disposed to sympathy and kindness. If you are a good man, you will surely find friends.”

“But that is the very root of my misery!” I cried, leaning forward in my earnestness. “I am, I believe, good. My heart is filled with love and benevolence. I have yearned for the affection and companionship of my fellows. But I am judged not by my heart, but by my appearance, which is, through no fault of my own, an object of horror to all who behold it. They see me and they flee, and I am left in a solitude more terrible than any punishment that was ever devised.”

A look of profound sympathy crossed the old man’s face. “My dear son,” he said, and the word ‘son’ was like a divine balm upon my wounds. “This is a sad story. I, too, have suffered from the injustice of the world. Men are often blinded by prejudice and superficialities. But do not despair. If you can find one person who is willing to look past these outward things and see the virtue within, you will have found a treasure. And where there is one, there may be others.”

My heart swelled to a bursting point. This was it! This was the moment of my salvation. He understood. He, in his wisdom and his darkness, saw the truth of me.

“You are right!” I exclaimed, my voice trembling with an emotion so powerful I could barely control it. “Oh, if I could but find such friends! I have, in my travels, observed a family for whom I have conceived the most ardent affection. They are virtuous and good, but they are poor and in exile. I have felt for them, and in my own small way, I have tried to assist them. But I am afraid to approach them. I fear their judgment. If they were to reject me, my heart would break.”

“Of whom do you speak?” he asked, a note of curiosity in his voice.

The sound of approaching footsteps and cheerful voices from the path outside sent a jolt of pure panic through me. It was too soon! They were returning! My plan was in ruins. I had not yet secured the old man’s promise.

“Now is the time!” I cried, in a voice of desperate supplication. I sprang from my stool and seized the old man’s hand. It was a rough, desperate gesture, and he started in surprise. “You must save and protect me! You and your family are the friends whom I seek! Do not desert me in this hour of trial!”

“Great God!” exclaimed the old man. “Who are you? Your hand is like ice, and your voice is filled with a terror I cannot comprehend!”

At that precise and terrible moment, the cottage door burst open. Felix, Agatha, and Safie stood upon the threshold, their faces rosy from the cold air, their arms full of wood. The light from the open door fell upon me, illuminating my features, my unnatural stature, my whole hideous and appalling form, as I knelt in desperate frenzy, clutching the hand of their father.

The moment stretched into an eternity of silence, a tableau of pure horror. Then the peace was shattered. A shrill shriek of terror erupted from Agatha, who, upon seeing me, fainted into her brother’s arms. Safie, unable to even scream, stood frozen, her eyes wide with a horror that surpassed even that of the agent I had driven away, before she turned and fled from the cottage. And Felix, his face a mask of rage and revulsion, sprang forward with a roar. He tore me away from his father, hurling me to the floor with a strength born of fury and fear. He then seized a heavy stick from the corner and advanced upon me, his intent clear.

Pain, a pain more profound than any physical blow, ripped through me. This was the result of my hopes. This was my reward for months of silent devotion. I could have torn him limb from limb, I could have laid the cottage and all its inhabitants to ruin in a single, blind burst of my accursed strength. But I did not. I uttered a howl of despair and agony, a sound so inhuman and full of sorrow that it seemed to come from the very depths of hell, and scrambling to my feet, I fled from the cottage. I ran, blind to my path, crashing through the undergrowth, the curses of Felix and the screams of Agatha echoing in my ears, pursuing me into the welcoming darkness of the forest and the deeper darkness of my own eternal despair.

Yet, a morbid and desperate curiosity, an unwilling tendril of my former attachment, compelled me to act. I could not quit the vicinity of the cottage without one last look, without knowing the full extent of the ruin I had wrought upon them and upon myself. The old man, De Lacey, sat in his armchair, his head bowed in his hands, the very picture of dejection. But it was the aspect of Felix that struck me with the greatest force. His countenance was hard and resolved, his eyes darting about the room as if expecting an attack at any moment. He held a pistol in his hand. He was speaking in a low, urgent tone to his father.

“My son,” the old man replied, his voice quavering, “you were too hasty. I did not see the creature, but I heard its voice. There was in it a misery so profound, a desperation so great… I felt its hand; it was cold, yes, but it was the hand of a supplicant, not an aggressor. Perhaps we have misjudged.”

“Misjudged!” cried Felix, his voice rising in disbelief. “Father, did you not hear Agatha’s shriek? Did you not see the terror that drove Safie from the house? I saw it! I saw its foul and demonic visage as it knelt before you. Its size, its deformity, its sheer unnaturalness… it is a thing of horror, a creature of malice. To think it has been lurking so near, watching us, for God knows how long! Every moment we remain is a moment we are in mortal danger. My decision is made. We will quit this cottage and seek our fortune elsewhere, where such abominations are not to be found.”

The old man sighed, a sound of deep and weary resignation. He could not contend with the terror of his children. My fate was sealed. I watched as they began to gather their few possessions. I heard the sounds of Agatha’s weeping and Felix’s attempts to comfort her, his words filled with execrations against the monster who had destroyed their peace. My own name, my own being, was now a curse upon their lips. I had sought to bring them joy, and I had brought them only ruin and fear. They were to be driven from their humble sanctuary, the only home they had known in their exile, and it was all my doing.

I remained at my post, a silent, unseen spectre of misery, and watched them for the remainder of the day. Towards evening, Felix having made some arrangement in the nearby village, a small cart arrived. With heavy hearts, they loaded their few articles of furniture and their personal belongings. I saw Felix lead his blind father to the cart, settling him as gently as he could. I saw Agatha, leaning heavily on Safie, her face still as white as death, climb slowly into the back. Their departure was a slow, mournful procession, a funeral for the life they had built and for the hopes I had so foolishly cherished. As the cart rumbled away down the lane, I felt a part of my own soul being torn from me. The sound of its wheels faded into the distance, and I was left alone with the silence, the empty cottage, and the vast, crushing weight of my solitude. The world was a vast and desolate void.

For a day and a night, I did not move from my hovel. I was as one dead, entombed in the ruins of my own heart. But on the second morning, a change came over me. The deep well of my sorrow began to dry up, and in its place, a scorching fire of rage began to burn. My thoughts, which had been a maelstrom of grief, now sharpened into a single point of incandescent fury. They had abandoned me. They had cursed me. Humanity had rejected me. Very well. If I could not inspire love, I would inspire fear. If I could not be a friend, I would be an enemy. This was the justice of the world, and I would now become its most devoted agent.

A dark and terrible resolution formed in my mind. The cottage, which had been the temple of my adoration, would now become the altar of my vengeance. It was a monument to my folly and their cruelty, and it must be utterly destroyed. As the sun began to set, I emerged from my hovel and began my work. I gathered dry branches and brushwood from the forest, the same forest that had once offered me shelter and solace. I worked with a feverish energy, piling the wood high against the walls of the cottage and the hovel that had been my miserable observatory. My heart beat with a wild and hideous glee. I was no longer the gentle, aspiring creature who had learned of virtue from the lips of Felix. I was a fiend, an avenger, and this was to be my first act of war against my enemies.

When night fell, a deep and starless blackness, I took a torch which I had lit from the embers of their abandoned fire. I gazed for a moment at the humble dwelling, the scene of all my joys and all my woes. Then, with a cry that was a mixture of a sob and a snarl, I thrust the flaming brand into the pyre I had constructed. The dry wood caught at once, and the flames leaped upwards with a hungry roar, licking at the dry thatch of the roof. I danced around the conflagration, my grotesque shadow capering in the flickering light. The fire was beautiful; it was a magnificent and terrible spectacle. It was the funeral pyre of my hopes and the birth of my despair. The flames rose to the heavens, a beacon of my hatred. As the cottage that had harboured all that I loved was consumed, I turned my back upon its ashes and swore an oath of eternal hatred and vengeance to all mankind, and above all, to him who had created me and sent me into this world of intolerable misery.

My mind was now fixed upon a single purpose: to find my creator and exact from him the justice that was my due. I had with me still the portmanteau I had found in the woods, containing not only the books that had given me language and ideas, but also a small collection of papers, a journal belonging to the man I now knew was my maker. I had perused them before, but in my innocence, I had not fully grasped their import. Now, by the dying light of the inferno I had made, I read them again. I learned of his family, of his studies, and of his home. A name was branded upon my mind: Geneva. It was there I must go. It was there I would find the author of my being. Oh, Frankenstein, be not surprised that I learned your name and your abode! You had left the damning evidence of your crime in the pocket of the coat you so carelessly discarded. You had given me the map to your own destruction.

I resolved to travel to Geneva, but my journey was to be one of hardship and renewed torment. The season was changing. The balmy nights of summer were gone, replaced by the sharp winds and driving rains of autumn. The leaves fell from the trees, leaving the woods bare and skeletal, a fitting mirror for the barren state of my own soul. I travelled only by night, subsisting on berries and roots, my heart a stone in my breast. The benignity I had once felt towards the world was replaced by a bitter and all-consuming misanthropy.

My hatred was nourished and strengthened by every encounter. One day, while seeking shelter from a sudden storm in the recesses of a thick wood, I heard the shrieks of a child. Following the sound, I saw a young girl who, having apparently slipped on the wet bank of a swift-flowing stream, had fallen into the water and was being carried away by the current. My first impulse, a lingering echo of my former self, was to save her. I plunged into the icy water, and with my superior strength, I battled the torrent and drew the child to the safety of the bank. I was in the act of attempting to restore her suspended animation when a man, no doubt her father, rushed towards us. Upon seeing me, a monster, bending over the body of his child, he did not pause to inquire or to thank. He uttered a savage cry, and wrenching the girl from my arms, he raised a musket to his shoulder and fired. A searing pain shot through my shoulder. I staggered back, a howl of pain and fury escaping my lips, and fled once more into the depths of the forest.

This was my reward for an act of compassion. I had saved a human life, and in return, I was wounded, cursed, and driven away like a rabid wolf. The wound in my flesh was painful, but it was nothing compared to the wound that this final, brutal act of injustice inflicted upon my spirit. If this was the nature of man, then I was right to despise him. My resolves were of adamant. Every feeling of sympathy, every last vestige of kindness, was extinguished in my heart. Vengeance, and vengeance alone, was now the sole passion of my existence.

The wound festered, and for many weeks I lay in a miserable shelter I constructed of branches, suffering the torments of fever and pain. My body healed, but my soul was scarred forever. When I was able to travel again, winter had set in. The earth was covered in a blanket of snow, and the rivers were frozen. My journey was slow and arduous. The cold that had once been a minor inconvenience was now a source of constant suffering, but I bore it, for my hatred was a fire that kept me from freezing. I was a solitary fiend, wandering through a frozen and hostile world, my purpose a cold, hard flame guiding me ever southwards.

After months of travel, of enduring hunger, cold, and the abhorrence of every living thing I chanced to meet, I at last saw the high, white peaks of the mountains that I knew, from the descriptions in your journal, surrounded your native city. I saw the glittering expanse of the lake and the distant spires of Geneva. A dark and triumphant feeling, a feeling of dreadful satisfaction, filled my breast. I was near my destination; I was near you. My long pilgrimage of hate was approaching its end, and a new and more terrible chapter was about to begin. I hid myself in the woods that bordered the city, a patient predator lying in wait, and I began to formulate the plan by which I would make you, my accursed creator, feel but a fraction of the agony that you had inflicted upon me. The world had made me a fiend; I would now show the world, and you, the full meaning of that word.

I was a solitary fiend, wandering through a frozen and hostile world, my purpose a cold, hard flame guiding me ever southwards.
