I found a wretched shelter in the thickest part of the woods on the slopes of Mont Salêve, a natural grotto concealed by a curtain of ivy and tangled undergrowth. From this vantage point, I could observe the roads leading to the city and, at times, catch a distant, glittering glimpse of the lake whose placid surface seemed to mock the tempest in my soul. I did not yet have a plan, only a purpose; a terrible, all consuming need for you to know I existed, not as a forgotten experiment, but as a power, a misery, a reckoning.

My days were passed in this grim watchfulness, my nights in foraging for the roots and berries that sustained my miserable existence. The memory of the cottagers, once a source of painful yearning, was now a wellspring of bitterness. Their simple virtues, their love, their gentleness; these were the qualities of a species to which I did not belong, a species I now vowed to injure. I thought of Felix’s lessons, of the history of man’s folly and greatness. I had wept with Safie for the vanquished peoples of the New World; now, I felt a kinship with them, for I too was a native driven from my own land, an original inhabitant of a world that refused to acknowledge me except with violence and scorn.

I learned the pathways and the habits of the local people by observing them from my hidden lairs. I saw lovers walking hand in hand at dusk, their soft laughter a torment to my ears. I saw groups of friends whose easy camaraderie was a dagger in my heart. I saw parents with their children, and the sight of such familial bliss would send me retreating into the deepest shadows of the wood, grinding my teeth and cursing the creator who had denied me all such bonds. My hatred for you, my author, grew with every passing hour, a monstrous edifice built brick by brick from the stolen joys I witnessed.

It was during one of these observations, on a fine evening in early spring, that my destiny took a more definite and dreadful shape. I had descended closer to the fields of Plainpalais, concealing myself within a thicket of hazel that bordered a well trodden path. A group from the city was enjoying the mild air, and my eye was drawn to two children who had run ahead of their guardians. They were boys, one of some seven years, the other a cherub of perhaps four or five, with golden hair and a countenance of angelic innocence. My gaze fixed upon the younger one; he was the very picture of the life and happiness from which I was forever outcast. A strange and terrible thought entered my mind, a whisper from the fiend that you had made of me. To extinguish such a light, to turn such joy into ashes; would that not be a worthy first stroke in my war against you and all mankind?

I watched as the older boy tired of their game and ran back to the adults, leaving the younger one to his own devices. The child, with the heedless curiosity of his age, began to chase a butterfly, his delighted laughter echoing through the tranquil evening. He strayed from the path, coming ever closer to my hiding place. My heart beat a strange and painful tattoo against my ribs, a mixture of dread and a horrifying, novel excitement. This was my moment. The world had presented me with a vessel for my vengeance.

I waited until he was but a few feet from the thicket, his back turned to me as he reached for a wildflower. With a speed that would have been imperceptible to a human eye, I emerged from the shadows and clasped my hand over his mouth, stifling the cry that rose in his throat. Instead, a kind of cruel power surged through me. Still, a vestige of my former self, the self that had longed for companionship, made a final, desperate plea. I spoke to him, my voice a low rumble, striving to keep the rage from it.

“Boy,” I said, “you must come with me. You shall be my companion. I mean you no harm, but you must be my friend. I am lonely, and all men hate me; but you are a child, and your heart has not yet learned such bitter lessons.”

Every injustice, every sorrow, every moment of agony coalesced into a single, blinding point of rage. This was not merely a random child; this was your relation. This was your kin, your blood, a part of the family that had lived in bliss while I suffered in solitude. My creator’s name, uttered as a threat, had become his death sentence.

I had made you feel, or I soon would, the same desolating grief that had been my only companion. I, the miserable creature, had exerted my power. I had created a sorrow that would ripple through your perfect world.

As I stood over my victim, my eye caught the glint of gold upon his chest. It was a locket, and I took it. Upon opening it, I beheld the miniature of a woman of surpassing beauty. It was your mother, I now know, a face of such gentle benevolence that it seemed to mock me from beyond the grave. Rage and envy filled me. I would not only commit the crime; I would orchestrate its aftermath. I would make your own systems of society my instruments of torture.

I needed a scapegoat, another victim to compound the tragedy and twist the knife of your suffering ever deeper.

I heard the frantic ringing of the church bells, a sound that was music to my ears. I saw the flicker of torches as search parties scoured the woods and fields, their desperate cries echoing in the night. I watched them find the body of the boy, and I savoured the wave of horror and grief that I knew was washing over your city, your home, your heart.

I had listened to conversations of passing travellers and learned that she had been discovered with the locket, accused, and cast into prison. I felt a sense of awesome, terrible power. I, the outcast, the monster, was pulling the strings, and the world of men was dancing to my tune of misery.

She was condemned, and your world, your family, was plunged into a new depth of sorrow. Two innocents destroyed, and all for me. All for my revenge.

I stood upon a crag of the Jura, the wind and rain lashing at my uncovered frame, and I felt not the cold but a burning, triumphant fire within. I had shown you what it was to feel loss. I needed you to know who was the author of your pain. I needed you to look upon my face again, not with the scientific curiosity of a creator, but with the terror and hatred of a victim.

I saw your hand instinctively fly to your breast, where I knew you kept a pistol, and a bitter smile, a contortion of my features which I have learned passes for a smile, crossed my lips. “Lay aside your weapons,” I said, my voice echoing strangely in the rarefied air, a sound neither human nor bestial, but a thing apart, like myself. “I do not mean to fight with you. My strength, as you well know, is superior to yours; my life is not so precious to me as to fear its loss. I am your creature; I am your Adam; but I am rather the fallen angel, whom you drive from joy for no misdeed. Everywhere I see bliss, from which I alone am irrevocably excluded. I was benevolent and good; misery made me a fiend. Make me happy, and I shall again be virtuous.”

You stood there, your form trembling not from the cold but from a rage so profound it rendered you speechless. Your lips moved, but only a hoarse, inarticulate sound escaped them. I continued, for now that I had begun, the torrent of my words could not be stayed. It was a flood that had been building for years in the desolate prison of my solitude.

“I ask of you a hearing,” I said, my tone shifting from one of demand to something that bordered on supplication. “Listen to me, Frankenstein. You accuse me of murder, and it is true, the blood of that innocent child is on my hands. But listen to my tale; listen to the chronicle of my hours of despair, my days of agonizing loneliness, and my nights of weeping. If you, after hearing my story, still desire my death, I shall offer no resistance. But if you feel, as I believe you must, some portion of the duty you owe to the being you brought into existence, you will not refuse my request. How can I move thee? Will no entreaties cause you to turn a favourable eye upon your creature, who implores your goodness and compassion?”

Your countenance was a storm of conflicting passions. I could see the hatred wrestling with a flicker of that old scientific curiosity, the horror of my presence warring with the undeniable truth of my words. You were my creator; what was I but the fruit of your ambition, the living consequence of your godlike presumption?

“Devil!” you cried at last, finding your voice. “You have made my world a desolation. The spirits of the murdered wander in this air and cry for vengeance. Begone! I will not hear you. There can be no community between you and me; we are enemies. Begone, or let us try our strength in a fight in which one of us must fall.”

“How can I be gone, and to what place?” I retorted, my patience wearing thin under the heat of your scorn. “Am I not alone, terribly alone? Felix had accidentally become acquainted with the Turk in Paris; the misfortunes of the latter had excited his warmest sympathy; and when the sentence of his new friend was promulgated, he had, with an ardour of generous indignation, resolved to rescue him from the power of his enemies. He had found means to communicate with the prisoner, had assisted him in his flight, and had finally conducted him, with his daughter, to a cottage in an obscure part of Germany.

Here the exiles had lived for some months in the deepest seclusion, when the arrival of my protectors had, in some measure, relieved their solitude. They had heard of the misfortunes of De Lacey, and had offered him their friendship and protection. The old man, blind and helpless, had gratefully accepted their kindness; and his children, though they mourned the loss of their former rank and fortune, had found in the society of each other, and in the exercise of their virtues, a degree of happiness which they had never known in the gay and dissipated circles of Paris. It was during this period that I first became a witness of their domestic economy, and an auditor of their conversations.

The narration of the fiend concluded, and the echoes of his final, dreadful threat seemed to hang in the frozen air, a curse made manifest. He stood before me, a colossal shape against the grey desolation of the ice, his form imbued with a terrible majesty, his words the pronouncements of an inexorable judge. A silence fell between us, more profound than any I had ever known, broken only by the groaning of the ice-floes and the whisper of the wind across the boundless waste. My own breath caught in my throat, a painful, ragged gasp. I felt the last vestiges of my strength abandon me, and a coldness, deeper even than that of the arctic frost, seeped into my bones.

“Devil!” I at last cried out, my voice a hoarse and broken thing, a mere shard of its former self. “You have related your catalogue of woes, and you have painted yourself a victim, an innocent Adam cast from a paradise he did not seek to corrupt. Do you think your eloquence can bewitch me? Do you imagine that a finely turned phrase can wash the blood of my brother from your hands? Can your artful tale of sorrow erase the image of my sweet Elizabeth, lifeless upon her bridal bier?”

My whole frame was seized with a paroxysm of rage that gave me a momentary, unnatural strength. I staggered to my feet, my limbs trembling not with cold, but with the violence of my detestation. “You speak of my duties,” I continued, my voice rising to a shrill scream that was snatched away by the wind. “What duty does a man owe to a pestilence? What compact can exist between the creator and the agent of his utter ruin? You call me a monster of selfishness, yet it was you who, denied one gratification, set out to annihilate every joy and every hope that warmed my heart. William was innocent. Justine was blameless. Clerval, my friend, the very brother of my soul, had shown you no malice. And Elizabeth, my more than life, my cherished consolation! You murdered them all, fiend, not from some grand principle of justice, but from a spite as base and as venomous as that of a trodden serpent.”

The creature did not move, but I could perceive, even in the dim light, the workings of his countenance. It was not remorse I saw there, but a settled and deliberate malevolence, a confirmation of all my deepest fears concerning his nature. He was not a being warped by circumstance; he was, and had always been, a vessel for evil.

“You demanded a companion,” I spat, the words tasting like poison in my mouth. “You asked that I should fashion a second creature as monstrous as yourself, to share in your exile. And for what purpose? That you might propagate a race of devils upon the earth, that your joint wickedness might spread like a plague, bringing terror and misery to all of humankind! I saw the flaw in your reasoning then, and I see it now. I did what was right. I destroyed the unholy thing upon my table to save millions yet unborn from the curse of your existence. That act was the single virtue of my wretched life, and I do not repent it. No, I glory in it! My only regret is that I did not, at that same moment, extinguish the spark of life within your own execrable frame.”

I raised my arm and pointed a trembling finger towards him, a gesture of ultimate condemnation. “You speak of your revenge. Your miserable and bloody tour of vengeance is as nothing to the sacred duty which now consumes me. You have taken from me every tie to my own species, you have made me a wanderer upon this desolate globe, but you have given me in return a singular and burning purpose. I am no longer a man of science, no longer a friend, a brother, a husband. I am an instrument of justice, a minister of retribution, and I have sworn an oath upon the graves of all I have lost that I shall not rest until I have hunted you down and torn you asunder, limb from limb!”

With this declaration, I drew from my coat the pistol I had kept always loaded, my hand shaking so violently that I could scarcely hold it. The creature watched the motion, and a terrible smile, a contortion of pure malice, twisted his features. “So, the creator raises his hand at last,” he said, his voice a low thunder that seemed to shake the very ice beneath my feet. “You have made your choice. But do you truly believe that your miserable weapon, or your own feeble strength, can be the instrument of my destruction? You are weak, Frankenstein. Your body is ravaged by toil and your mind by grief. I am as I was on the day of my creation, endowed with a strength and an agility that you cannot comprehend. Your hunt is over. He took a step towards me, and I, in a fit of desperate fury, pulled the trigger. The report of the pistol shot was a deafening crack in the immense silence, but the ball whizzed harmlessly past his head. Before I could even register my failure, he was in motion. He did not rush me, as I had expected; instead, with a laugh that was the most horrific sound I had ever heard, a sound of triumph and derision, he turned and sprang away from me. He leaped across a wide chasm in the ice with an ease that was more than human, landing upon the opposing floe.

He turned back to face me across the newly opened gulf of black, churning water. “Follow me, creator!” he called out, his voice carrying clearly over the moaning wind. “Pursue me across the roof of the world! And with another booming laugh, he turned and fled, his immense figure diminishing with incredible speed into the grey mists of the polar twilight. I shrieked with impotent rage and despair, and fired my second pistol after him, the ball once more finding no mark but the empty air. I then cast the useless weapon from me and attempted to follow, but my first step brought me to the edge of the chasm. I fell to my knees, staring into the dark, icy water that separated me from my nemesis. He was gone, a phantom swallowed by the wilderness, and I was left alone with my hatred and my exhaustion.

For a long time I knelt there, the cold penetrating my very marrow, my mind a vortex of agony. The spirits of the dead seemed to rise up from the frozen depths to surround me. I saw the gentle face of my father, his white hair stained with the sorrow I had brought upon him. I saw Clerval, his eyes full of the life and intellectual fire that I had indirectly extinguished. I saw Elizabeth, my celestial love, her countenance pale and her expression one of sublime and sorrowful reproach. And I saw William, my little brother, his innocent features contorted in terror. They did not speak, but their silent condemnation was a torment more severe than any physical pain. “This is your work,” they seemed to say. “This desolation, within and without, is the fruit of your unhallowed ambition.”

A groan of utter misery escaped my lips, but it was not a groan of surrender. The vision of my lost ones, far from crushing my spirit, inflamed it anew. My purpose was not for myself alone; it was for them. It was the only atonement I could offer for their fates. I rose once more, my body an instrument of pure will. I searched the horizon for any sign of my foe, but saw nothing but the endless expanse of ice and snow. I knew, however, the general direction he had taken, northwards, always northwards, into the heart of eternal winter.

My days thereafter became a monotonous cycle of torment and pursuit. The creature, in his diabolical cruelty, took care that I should not perish too quickly. When my meagre provisions were exhausted, I would find, left upon a prominent ridge of ice, a dead hare or a sea bird, and a mocking inscription scratched into the surface nearby: “Your sustenance, creator. Eat, and regain your strength for the chase.” My soul recoiled from this sustenance provided by my tormentor, yet I ate, for to die would be to grant him the victory. I choked down the raw flesh, and the nourishment it gave me felt like a further pollution of my being.

I travelled by the dim light of the perpetual arctic day, my sledge dogs growing weaker, my own body assailed by the unceasing cold. At night, or what passed for night in that land, I would sometimes see him, a distant silhouette upon a mountain of ice, observing me. He would not allow me to approach, but his presence was a constant reminder, a goad to my exhausted spirit. Sometimes, the aurora would blaze in the sky above, and its ghastly, shifting light would illuminate his form, making him appear like some vast demon presiding over a world of death.

During these endless days of pursuit, my mind, weakened by fatigue and despair, began to play tricks upon me. I was assailed by waking dreams of the most vivid and terrible kind. I would see the creature’s face in the patterns of the snow, hear his voice in the howling of the wind. I conversed with the ghosts of my family, arguing my case before them, pleading for their forgiveness, and renewing my vows of vengeance in their spectral presence. I lost all track of time, of days and weeks; my world shrank to the single, obsessive thought of the chase, the white landscape before me, and the dark figure that always remained just beyond my reach.

On one occasion, I awoke from a brief and troubled sleep to find another of his messages. This one was not accompanied by food. It was merely a few words carved into the ice beside my sledge. “I am approaching my journey’s end,” it read. “You are slow, Frankenstein. I grow weary of this game. Come, let us finish it.” The words filled me with a desperate, renewed energy. Was it possible? Was he, too, feeling the effects of this inhuman journey? The hope, however faint, that his preternatural strength might have its limits, was like a draught of strong wine to my famished spirit. I urged my remaining dogs forward with a frenzied cry, my eyes scanning the horizon for the final confrontation I so desperately craved.

The landscape changed. The vast, flat ice-floes gave way to a chaotic jumble of shattered ice mountains and deep, treacherous crevasses. My sledge became useless, and two of my last three dogs perished, falling into a fissure that opened suddenly beneath their feet. I was forced to abandon my sledge and the few remaining supplies, and to continue on foot, armed with only my indomitable will and the pistol I had recovered.

It was in this state, alone, starving, and half-crazed with my ordeal, that I finally saw it. Not the creature, but something far more unexpected. A shape on the horizon, dark against the ice, a form that was too regular, too structured, to be a work of nature. With a heart pounding with a mixture of hope and disbelief, I stumbled towards it. As I drew nearer, the shape resolved itself into the masts and rigging of a ship, trapped and enclosed by the ice.

A cry of human sound, the first I had uttered in what seemed an eternity that was not a shriek of rage or a groan of despair, escaped my lips. I ran, I stumbled, I fell and rose again, my eyes fixed upon that vessel as a dying man in the desert fixes his gaze upon a mirage of an oasis. It was not salvation I sought, not a return to the world of men which I had forsaken and which had forsaken me. It was a means, an instrument. If I could reach these men, I could tell them my story. I could warn them of the fiend that stalked this frozen wasteland. And if I should perish, if my strength should finally fail me, perhaps I could enlist them in my sacred quest. One of them might take up my burden, might become the arm of that justice which I had so long striven to enact.

My strength gave out within sight of the ship. I collapsed upon the snow, my vision blurring, the sounds of the world fading into a dull roar. Yet as my consciousness ebbed away, I saw figures detaching themselves from the ship, men running towards me across the ice. My last conscious thought was not one of gratitude, but a silent, desperate prayer: that they would understand, that they would believe, and that they would not fail where I had failed.

And so, Walton, you and your men found me, a wretched ruin of a man, clinging to the last embers of a life consumed by its own fire. You took me in, you warmed my frozen limbs, and you listened with astonishment to the fevered fragments of my tale. Now you have heard the whole of it, from the first spark of my unhallowed ambition in Ingolstadt to this final, desperate chase upon the desolate sea of ice. You see before you not a man seeking rescue, but a being who has a task to perform. I do not ask for your pity; I demand your aid. When I have recovered some measure of my strength, I must leave your vessel and continue my pursuit. But if I should die, Walton, if this fever should consume me, I adjure you, I command you, to take up my cause. Swear to me that if the fiend should appear, you will not be swayed by his words, but will execute the vengeance that is due. Swear to me, Walton, that you will be the instrument of my final justice. For on this desolate stage of ice, the drama must find its end, and either he or I must be destroyed.

His words yet echoed in my ears; his final, terrible demand hung in the frozen air between us like a suspended blade. Swear an oath, he had said; swear that you will become the instrument of my justice.

I looked upon the man before me, this magnificent ruin, this mind of unparalleled genius now shackled to a body which fever and grief had brought to the very precipice of the grave. Was this, then, the end of my great ambition? I had sailed northwards seeking glory, a passage to unknown lands, and a friend with whom I might share the raptures of my soul. I had found that friend, and his soul was indeed a thing of wonder, but a wonder blighted and consumed. The glory I sought seemed now a child’s bauble, a vain and foolish fancy when set against the immensity of this man’s suffering. His story, so wild, so fantastical, and yet told with an accent of such desperate, heart-rending truth, had seized upon my mind and would not let it go. The universe I had known, a world of ordered science and benevolent nature, had been torn asunder, and in its place was a cosmos of dark creation and dreadful, solitary woe.

Could I believe him? Every rational part of my mind cried out against the possibility of such a narrative; and yet, how could I not? The evidence was before me, not in proofs, but in the living testament of his own destruction. No common grief could have etched such lines of agony upon a human countenance; no ordinary tale of woe could have kindled such a fire of ceaseless vengeance in a human heart. I had seen the creature, or so I believed, in that fleeting glimpse across the ice, a figure of gigantic stature, inhumanly swift, which had lent a terrifying credence to the first words my guest had uttered upon this vessel.

And now this oath. To hunt down and destroy a being, a creature which, if Frankenstein’s own words were true, possessed reason, feeling, and a misery that mirrored his creator’s own. My blood ran cold at the thought. It was a task for an avenging angel, not a mortal man whose sole purpose hitherto had been the expansion of knowledge and the betterment of mankind. Yet as I gazed upon Victor’s pale, sweat-sheened brow, as I heard his shallow, laboured breaths, a profound pity, mingled with a strange and terrible admiration, took possession of my soul. He was my friend; I had bound myself to him. His enemy, by some unwritten law of fellowship, must therefore be my own.

“Rest now, my dearest friend,” I said at last, my voice thick with an emotion I could not conceal. I took his hand, which was hot and dry with fever. “You have exhausted yourself. We will speak more of this when your strength has returned. For now, allow me to be your nurse; let my care be the first token of my devotion to you.”

A faint smile, more sorrowful than any expression of grief I have ever witnessed, played upon his lips. “My strength will not return, Walton,” he whispered, his voice barely audible above the groaning of the ship’s timbers. “This fire has consumed its fuel; only the embers remain, and they, too, will soon be cold. You are my last hope. Do not fail me.” He said no more, but fell into a troubled, feverish slumber, his broken murmurs filled with the names of those he had loved and lost: Elizabeth, Clerval, William.

The days that followed, my sister, were the most trying of my life. Our ship remained locked in the unyielding embrace of the ice, a silent, white prison under a sky of pale, unending grey. The spirits of the crew, already low, sank into a state of sullen despair, which soon began to curdle into open discontent. They watched my ministrations to Frankenstein with suspicion and resentment. They saw him not as the noble, tragic figure I knew, but as a madman whose ill-omened presence had brought this curse of ice upon us. The mate, a good and steady man but one of little imagination, approached me one evening as I stood upon the deck, staring out at the hopeless expanse.

“Captain,” he began, his tone respectful yet firm, “the men are growing restless. The ice shows no sign of yielding, and our provisions, while yet sufficient, will not last forever in this frozen hell. They speak of turning back. They say this voyage is doomed.” He paused, then gestured with his head towards my cabin. “And they speak of him. They fear his madness is a contagion, and that your care for him has blinded you to our peril.”

“He is not mad, Mr. Saville,” I replied, with more sharpness than I intended. “He is a man who has suffered more than any ten men should have to bear. We owe him our compassion, our aid.”

“Compassion, yes, Captain,” he answered, “but we owe our lives to our own prudence. To remain here is to court death for the sake of one man’s vendetta. They are demanding that you give the order to abandon this quest and steer for home as soon as the ice permits.”

Was I not, in my devotion to Frankenstein, betraying the trust of these men who had placed their lives in my hands? Was my own ambition, now transferred to Victor’s cause, to be the ruin of us all? I dismissed the mate with a promise to consider his words, but my heart was a tempest of conflicting duties. My promise to my crew, and that terrible, unspoken oath to my dying friend.

I returned to the cabin to find Victor awake, his eyes strangely clear and bright. He seemed to have overheard, or perhaps to have divined, the nature of my conversation on the deck.

“They wish to turn back, do they not?” he asked, a note of bitter irony in his voice. “They wish to return to their warm hearths and their smiling families, and to leave the fiend to his work of evil. So be it. Let them flee. But you, Walton, you are made of sterner stuff. You spoke to me once of your thirst for glory, of your willingness to sacrifice all for some great and noble purpose. Is this not such a purpose? To rid the world of a monster, a creature whose existence is a perpetual stain upon the face of creation?”

His words ignited a spark of my old self, the self that had dreamed of planting a flag on the northernmost point of the earth. He saw my hesitation, my internal struggle, and his expression softened.

“Ah, Walton,” he sighed, “you are a good man. Your heart is not hardened, as mine has been, by years of solitary vengeance. You see the peril, the risk to your men, and you hesitate. I do not blame you. Perhaps I am wrong to ask this of you. Perhaps it is my fate, and mine alone, to bear this burden. But when you think of me, when you return to your safe and happy England, remember my story. Remember what becomes of those who, in their pride and arrogance, presume to usurp the power of the Almighty. Let my ruin be your lesson.”

He turned his face to the wall, and I felt a shame so profound that I could not speak. He believed I was abandoning him, that I was choosing the safety of my crew over the justice he so desperately craved. In that moment, all my doubts were swept away. My course was set.

I sat with him, I bathed his brow, I listened to the outpourings of a soul in its final agony

I have learned the great and terrible lesson of my friend’s life: that the pursuit of knowledge without wisdom, of creation without love, leads only to destruction. I return to you a sadder and a wiser man. I hope you will still receive your brother, who has looked into the abyss and has, by the grace of God, been permitted to return.
